event: I made a small mistake while introducing myself at a networking event.
rawInterpretation: Everyone noticed and thinks I am awkward.
alternateRealityChecks: Most people are primarily focused on themselves during social events.
Minor mistakes are often forgotten quickly by others.
People generally judge themselves more harshly than they judge strangers.
There is no evidence that others formed a negative opinion.
revisedInterpretation: The mistake was likely far more noticeable to me than to anyone else.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Several people connected with me afterwards and did not mention the mistake.

event: I sent a message to a group chat and nobody responded.
rawInterpretation: People are ignoring me because they do not like me.
alternateRealityChecks: Group messages are often overlooked.
People may not know how to respond.
A lack of response does not automatically indicate dislike.
Many unrelated factors could explain the silence.
revisedInterpretation: The lack of replies may be unrelated to how people feel about me.
chosenBehaviour: Avoid making assumptions based on silence.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Several people later responded once the conversation became active again.

event: I arrived at a gathering and people continued talking without acknowledging me immediately.
rawInterpretation: Nobody is happy that I came.
alternateRealityChecks: People may have been focused on an ongoing conversation.
The absence of a greeting does not imply rejection.
Social attention is often delayed in larger groups.
There is insufficient evidence to conclude that people are unhappy to see you.
revisedInterpretation: The situation may be explained by the flow of the conversation rather than how people feel about me.
outcomeOneWeekLater: People engaged enthusiastically once I joined the discussion.

event: I told a joke and nobody laughed.
rawInterpretation: People think I am boring and unfunny.
alternateRealityChecks: Humour is highly contextual.
People may have been distracted or tired.
One joke does not define your personality.
Not every joke lands, even for professional comedians.
revisedInterpretation: The joke simply did not work in that moment.
chosenBehaviour: Let it go and continue participating.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Nobody appeared to remember the incident.

event: I saw photos online from an event that I was not invited to.
rawInterpretation: Nobody considers me a close friend.
alternateRealityChecks: Not every social gathering includes every friend.
Attendance may have been limited by practical constraints.
Being excluded from one event does not reflect all relationships.
Friendship cannot be accurately measured by a single invitation.
revisedInterpretation: Being left out of one event does not define my social value.
chosenBehaviour: Avoid drawing broad conclusions from a single event.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Friends invited me to another gathering.

event: People seemed distracted while I was speaking.
rawInterpretation: What I am saying is not interesting.
alternateRealityChecks: Attention can be influenced by many factors unrelated to the speaker.
People may have personal concerns occupying their thoughts.
A distracted listener does not necessarily reflect content quality.
Their behaviour does not provide enough evidence about their opinions.
revisedInterpretation: The distraction may not be related to me or my contribution.
chosenBehaviour: Continue speaking normally rather than self-censoring.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Several people later referenced points I had made.

event: A friend took several hours to reply to my message.
alternateRealityChecks: People often respond when they have time and energy.
Message delays are common.
There is no direct evidence that the delay reflects anger.
Multiple explanations remain possible.
revisedInterpretation: I do not know why the reply was delayed.
outcomeOneWeekLater: My friend replied and apologised for being busy.

event: I felt nervous and awkward during a conversation with new people.
alternateRealityChecks: Feeling awkward occasionally is a normal human experience.
Comfort often increases as people become familiar.
One interaction does not define social ability.
Most people experience uncertainty in unfamiliar situations.
revisedInterpretation: I felt uncomfortable in this situation, but that does not mean I am bad at socialising.

event: A group of people stopped talking when I approached.
alternateRealityChecks: Conversations naturally change when someone new joins.
There is no evidence that the discussion involved you.
People often pause conversations to include newcomers.
Assumptions are not facts.
revisedInterpretation: Their behaviour does not provide enough information to know what they were discussing.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The conversation turned out to be about a topic unrelated to me.

event: I was not tagged in a friend's social media post.
rawInterpretation: They do not value our friendship.
alternateRealityChecks: Social media behaviour does not always reflect relationship quality.
People have different habits regarding tagging and posting.
One online action does not define a friendship.
Additional evidence would be needed to support that conclusion.
revisedInterpretation: The post alone does not provide enough information about the friendship.
chosenBehaviour: Focus on real-world interactions rather than online signals.
outcomeOneWeekLater: My friend continued to engage normally and positively.

event: Over the past month, several friends have met up multiple times without inviting me.
rawInterpretation: They no longer want me in their friend group.
alternateRealityChecks: The repeated pattern makes it reasonable to feel concerned.
There may be practical reasons for some of the gatherings.
The available information does not explain why you were not included.
The situation may warrant a conversation rather than assumptions.
revisedInterpretation: I have noticed a pattern that is worth understanding, but I do not know the reasons behind it.
chosenBehaviour: Discuss the situation with a trusted friend rather than speculating.
outcomeOneWeekLater: One friend explained that the recent gatherings were organised around a shared hobby that I had never expressed interest in.

event: I introduced myself to someone and they seemed uninterested in continuing the conversation.
rawInterpretation: I made a bad impression and people generally do not enjoy talking to me.
alternateRealityChecks: You only observed one brief interaction.
The other person may have been tired, distracted, or preoccupied.
Chemistry varies between individuals and situations.
One interaction cannot define how people generally experience you.
revisedInterpretation: The conversation may simply not have connected, and that does not reflect my overall social ability.
chosenBehaviour: Continue meeting new people rather than focusing on one interaction.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Several later conversations felt natural and enjoyable.

event: People laughed shortly after I walked away from a conversation.
alternateRealityChecks: You do not know the content of the conversation.
People laugh for many reasons unrelated to others.
The timing may be coincidental.
There is no direct evidence that the laughter was about you.
revisedInterpretation: I cannot know what the laughter was about based solely on timing.
chosenBehaviour: Avoid filling gaps in information with assumptions.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The topic of conversation turned out to be unrelated.

event: I attended a party where I knew very few people and struggled to join conversations.
rawInterpretation: I do not fit in socially.
alternateRealityChecks: Many people find unfamiliar social situations uncomfortable.
Joining existing groups often requires time and persistence.
Difficulty in one environment does not define social identity.
The context itself may have contributed to the discomfort.
revisedInterpretation: The situation was challenging, but it does not mean I am incapable of fitting in socially.
chosenBehaviour: Keep attending social events and focus on small interactions.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Future events felt easier as familiarity increased.

event: A friend repeatedly interrupts me and rarely asks questions about my life during conversations.
rawInterpretation: They do not care about me as a friend.
alternateRealityChecks: The behaviour appears to be recurring rather than a single incident.
Some people are poor conversational listeners without intending harm.
It is reasonable to examine whether the friendship feels balanced.
The behaviour may indicate a problem, but it does not automatically reveal the person's intentions.
revisedInterpretation: There may be an issue in how our conversations work, and it is worth discussing rather than assuming they do not care.
chosenBehaviour: Talk openly about how the conversations make me feel.
outcomeOneWeekLater: My friend was surprised by the feedback and made an effort to be more attentive.
